paragraphs.text: ON THE LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY THE WONDERWORKER. Our discourse and our present gathering have one and the same aim. Gregory the Great is set before you as the reason for this assembly, and before me as the subject of this address. I think it takes the same power to achieve virtue in deed as to tell of noble things worthily in words. So we should call on the same help through which he achieved virtue in his life. In my judgment, that help is the grace of the Spirit, which by itself strengthens those who have laboured at either, whether in living or in speaking. That brilliant and admired life was achieved by the power of the Spirit. It is therefore a matter for prayer that as much help may come to this discourse as came to him in his life. Then the praise will not be found to fall short of the worth of his achievements, and through this remembrance the man may be shown to those present just as he himself was seen in his deeds by the people of his own time. Now if remembering those who excel in virtue brought no profit, and contributed nothing toward the good for those who hear, it would perhaps be superfluous and useless to turn one's speech to praise with no useful end, going through it in vain and idly wearying the ears. But such a gracious discourse, if it is done fittingly, will bring a common profit to the hearers, just as a beacon guides toward itself those sailing in from the sea who are wandering in the darkness of the open water. So I think equal zeal is needed for this on both sides, from you in listening and from me in speaking. For it is clear that his virtuous life, shining like a beacon upon our souls through memory, becomes a road to the good both for the one who tells of it and for those who hear. We human beings are somehow made so that we want to make our own everything that is praiseworthy and honourable, and come to desire to possess it. Such, then, is the subject of my words. And for me there is no danger at all in venturing upon it, whether my discourse proves able to rise to the greatness of the deeds

or not. Either way the praise will match the one being praised. If the discourse reaches the height of his wonders, it will surely astonish the ear with his achievements. If it falls short of their greatness, even so the glory of the one praised is made brighter. For the best praise of a man is to be shown greater than the power of those who praise him. But let no one schooled in divine wisdom expect, after the custom of outsiders, that one who is praised spiritually should be praised by the technical methods of the encomium. For we and others do not judge what is good by the same standards. Nor would one find the same opinions [?] about the same things among those who live according to the world and those who have risen above the world. To the former, the things that seem great and worth striving for are wealth, lineage, glory, worldly power, myths about the founding of their native cities, and stories that sensible people would shun: trophies and battles and the evils of war. In our teaching, however, only one fatherland is honoured: paradise, the first hearth of the human race. There is only one city, the heavenly one, built of living stones, whose craftsman and maker is God. There is only one dignity of birth, kinship with God. This does not come to someone by chance, like worldly nobility, which by that same automatic succession often flows down even to the base. It can be acquired in no other way than by free choice. 'For as many as received him,' says the divine voice, 'to them he gave power to become children of God.' What could be more dignified than such nobility? For all others, ancestral traditions are myths and fictions, with deceits of demons mixed into the mythical tales. Our ancestral heritage, however, needs no storytellers. Anyone who looks at the sky and its beauties, and contemplates the whole creation with the eye of the soul, will find that all the wonders he can grasp in these things are the stories of our fatherland. Or rather, they are not stories of the fatherland itself, but of the colony: we were sent out as colonists from the higher life, and have settled in this present world. And if the colony is like this, one must consider what the mother city of the colony is like: what beauty there is in it, what its palaces are like, what blessedness belongs to those who have been granted a dwelling there. If the visible things of creation are such as to be beyond praise, what must one think of what surpasses them, which the eye cannot grasp, nor the ear take in, nor the mind conjecture? Through this spiritual praise of those he praises, the divine [?] of encomia rejects the trifles of this world below. He judges it shameful that those who are known for such things should be glorified for what is valued on earth.

Let a worldly man, whose eyes are on material prosperity, gather praise for people from such things: whether someone's native land is rich in livestock, whether a neighbouring sea supplies gluttons with abundant provisions [?], whether stone laid upon stone beautifies the buildings. But one who looks to the life above will count ambition for earthly things a disgrace. For him, beauty is purity of soul, wealth is having no possessions, fatherland is virtue, and his city is the very palace of God. So we too will stand aloof from praise of this kind. We will not add his native land to the praises of Gregory the Great, nor will we bring in ancestors as allies of our encomium. We know that no praise is true unless it belongs to the person praised as his own. And by 'his own' we mean what remains entirely and forever beyond being taken away. We are separated from everything: wealth, distinction, glory, honour, luxury, enjoyment, kinsmen, friends. Only our disposition toward vice or virtue stays with us. Therefore we judge only the virtuous man blessed. And let no one suppose that I have nothing distinguished to tell about the man's native land or ancestors, and am stealthily hiding the shame of it under a pretence of disregarding such things. Who does not know the name of the sea, which all people have given to that nation in particular, and which bears witness to the virtue of those who held that land from the beginning? Of all lands and seas, this sea alone is called the Euxine, the 'hospitable' sea. Perhaps the name testifies to their kindness toward the strangers who visit them. Or perhaps it is because the land is such that it generously bestows the means of life not only on natives and those born in the land, but also on those who come to it from everywhere. For the nature of the country is such that it produces everything necessary for life and lacks none of the good things found elsewhere, since the sea makes everything from everywhere their own. The whole nation is such that whatever part of it one examines by itself, one thinks it surpasses the others. Nonetheless, by the common judgment of the nation, the city of the great Gregory is like a crown over the whole surrounding region. A distinguished emperor, one of those who strengthened Roman rule, named Caesar, was so captivated by love and longing for the country that he saw fit to have the city called Neocaesarea after his own name. But these things have nothing to do with our aim. We do not suppose that they make that great one among the saints more distinguished: whether the land is laden with fruit, whether the city is adorned with buildings, or whether goods from everywhere are freely brought in by the neighbouring sea to satisfy any fancy.

Nor will I mention in my discourse his ancestors, who came before him in his birth according to the flesh, by recounting their wealth, their lavish gifts and their worldly distinctions. What would these contribute to the praise of one who raised himself above the whole world: tombs and monuments and inscriptions and stories of the dead? Besides, it is not possible to give a share in the praise to those whose kinship he renounced, as far as kinship of the soul is concerned. For they were made futile in the error of idols. He, however, looked up to the truth and through faith adopted himself into the kinship above. So we pass over how he was born, or from whom, or what city he first lived in, since these contribute nothing to our present purpose. We shall begin our praise where he began the virtuous life. His parents ended their lives while he was still very young in body, so he was left without the care that nature provides. That is the age when the mind, still immature, goes wrong in judging the good in most people. Yet from the very first he showed what he would become in the fullness of his years. Noble young plants, when they shoot up from their first growth into straight branches, show the farmers in the present season the beauty they will have later. In the same way, at an age when the souls of others are unsteady through ignorance, and youth for the most part slips readily toward vain and useless things, he showed in himself, by the first choice of his life, that David spoke truly: 'The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree.' For this alone among trees springs up from the earth with its crown already at full thickness. As it grows in height, it receives no addition in breadth over time. So he too flowered from his first shoot, rising at once complete and lofty-crowned in his choice of life. He stood aloof from everything that excites the young: horsemanship, hunting, finery, clothes, dice, luxury. At once he devoted himself wholly to acquiring the virtues, always choosing in turn what suited his age at the time. The first virtue he pursued was zeal for wisdom. Temperance followed alongside it, like a colt yoked to it, and self-control was an ally to both. His freedom from pride and anger was achieved together with his contempt for money. For arrogance and pride have no other origin than greed, which brings such passions in with it. And just as the account goes of

the patriarch Abraham, that he became learned in the philosophy of the Chaldeans and observed the harmonious and ordered positions and movements of the stars. He used his knowledge of these as a stepping-stone toward the contemplation of the transcendent good, reasoning: if the things perceptible to the senses are like this, what must the things beyond the senses be? So he attained what he sought, as though he had climbed upon outside wisdom and been raised higher by it, so as to come near in some way to what cannot be grasped. In the same way this Great one diligently engaged with outside philosophy, and was led to an understanding of Christianity by the very things through which most people are confirmed in paganism. He left the erring worship of his fathers and sought the truth of what really exists, taught the incoherence of the pagan doctrines by the very labours of the outsiders. He saw that Greek and barbarian philosophy alike were split into differing opinions in their views about the Divine. Their leading teachers did not agree with one another, and each contended to strengthen his own position by the ingenuity of his arguments. So he left them, overthrowing one another like men in a civil war. Instead he took hold of the steadfast word of faith. That word is not strengthened by any logical subtlety or technical intricacy, but is proclaimed equally to all in simple words, and its very credibility lies in its being beyond belief. If what it says could be grasped by the power of human reasoning, it would be no different from Greek wisdom. For they too suppose that whatever they are able to grasp is what exists. But the transcendent nature cannot be reached and comprehended by human reasoning. For this reason faith takes the place of reasoning, reaching out toward what is beyond reason and comprehension. Scripture says of Moses that he was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. In the same way this Great one went through the whole of Greek education, learned by experience how weak and incoherent their doctrines were, and became a disciple of the Gospel. Even before he was brought through the mystical and incorporeal birth, he ordered his life so well that he brought no stain of sin with him to the washing. He was living in Egypt, in the great city of Alexander, where young people zealous for philosophy and medicine flocked together from everywhere. To his contemporaries he was a hard sight to bear: a young man adorned with self-control beyond his years. For the praise of the pure was a reproach to the defiled. So the licentious wanted to have an excuse, that they might not seem to be the only ones of that kind. Out of malice they contrived a scheme to rub some blemish onto the life of the Great one. To slander him they put forward a common courtesan, from a brothel, (Acts [?])

notorious for her disgrace. As was his custom, he was examining and discussing some philosophical question with learned men in a dignified manner. The woman came up to him, simpering and coquettish, and by everything she said and did she pretended in every way to be on familiar terms with him. Then she said she had been cheated of her wages, and shamelessly added the occasions for which she claimed the payment had been withheld. Those who knew his pure life were indignant and stirred to anger against the woman. But he was not disturbed along with those who were angry on his behalf, nor did he say anything that a man vexed at being slandered would be likely to say. He did not call witnesses to his way of life, did not fend off the blemish with an oath, and did not expose the malice of those who had contrived this against him. Instead, in a calm and steady voice, he turned to one of his companions and said, 'My friend, pay her the money, so that she does not trouble us any longer and disturb the discussion we are engaged in.' The man he had instructed learned from the courtesan how much money she was demanding of him, and readily counted out the whole sum. The plot of the licentious against the chaste man had reached its end, and the gain was already in the hands of the disreputable woman. Then indeed there came from God both testimony to the young man's chastity and refutation of his contemporaries' slander. The moment she received the money in her hand, she was racked by a demonic spirit. She howled with a bestial roar instead of a human voice and fell headlong in the midst of the gathering, suddenly becoming a horrifying and fearful sight to those present. Her hair was flung about and torn by her own hands, her eyes rolled back, and her mouth spewed foam. And the demon that was choking her did not let her go until that Great one called upon God and appeased him on her behalf. Such are the stories of the great man's youth, truly worthy preludes to the life he lived afterward. And yet the wonder is so great that, even if there were nothing else to tell besides, this alone would make him second to none [?] of those who have excelled in virtue. He was rich and young, living abroad in a populous city where the young lived freely in pleasures, so that the purity of the chaste was a reproach to the foolish. There was no mother to

concern herself with his life, no father to guide his daily conduct. Yet through freedom from passion he raised himself so high toward virtue that he made the overseer of the universe the witness of his life, who refuted the woman's slander by that grievous stroke. What greater subject for praise could anyone conceive? How could anyone admire him as he deserves? By reason he wrestled nature to the ground, and yoked his youth to reason like one of the tame animals. He became stronger than all the natural passions that rise up. He stirred against himself the envy that grows upon everything good, and became stronger than that too. He did not rise up to retaliate against the plot of his companions. Instead he did good to the woman who had served them in their slander, delivering her through prayer from the affliction of the demon. Such we know Joseph to have been from the history. Lawless conduct with his master's wife lay open to him whenever he wished, for she herself was mad for the young man's beauty, and no human being was there to witness the attempt. But he too looked to the divine eye and chose to seem wicked rather than to become wicked, undergoing the lot of criminals rather than becoming a criminal. But perhaps there is something in which this man may boast even more than that history. For when it comes to shunning defilement, the abomination of adultery is not the same as what seems to carry the blame of a lesser fault. Here there was no danger from the laws. Yet he judged the pleasure that comes from sin to be in itself more fearful than punishment. So either he surpassed Joseph by the greatness of this wonder, or he will certainly not be judged second to him. Such, then, was the prelude to his life. But what was the life itself? When he had run through the whole education of outside wisdom, he met Firmilian, a Cappadocian of noble family, whose character was like his own, as Firmilian showed by his later life when he became the ornament of the Church of Caesarea. Gregory made clear to his friend the aim of his mind and of his own life, that he was looking toward God. He learned that his friend's zeal agreed with his in the same desire. Then he left all his zeal for outside philosophy, and together with Firmilian he went to study under the man who at that time led the philosophy of the Christians. This was Origen, who is much talked of for his writings. By this, too, Gregory showed not only his love of learning and hard work but also the restraint and modesty of his character. Though he was full of so much wisdom, he did not think it beneath him to use another teacher for divine studies. He spent as much time with the teacher as his studies required. Many people urged him to stay and tried to keep him in that foreign land, asking him to remain with them. But he preferred the land that bore him above everything, and returned to his native country, bringing with him the manifold wealth of wisdom and knowledge, which like a merchant

[?] …in his secular studies, he had moved among all who were held in high esteem. And yet anyone who judges fairly will surely count this, too, as no small ground for praise: that he disregarded so great a supplication made by a whole city together, and the eagerness of all its leading men that he should stay, and the zeal of the governors residing among them for this same end. All of them aimed that the great man should remain with them, to be, as it were, a founder of virtue and a lawgiver of life. But he fled on every side from whatever feeds vanity, knowing that the passion of pride is for the most part the origin of a life of vice, and he made for the quiet life in his homeland as for a harbour. The whole nation looked to him, and all expected him to display his learning publicly in common assemblies, so that he might reap the renown it would bring as the fruit of his long labours. But that great man knew how true philosophy ought to be displayed by those who pursue it in earnest, so that the soul may never be wounded by ambition (for the praise of listeners has a terrible power to slacken the soul's vigour with vanity and love of glory). For this reason he made silence his display, showing the treasure within by deeds, not words. He separated himself from the bustle of the marketplace and from city life altogether, and in some remote place he lived alone with himself, and through himself with God. He made small account of the whole world and all that is in it. He did not busy himself with kingdoms or look into the offices of state, and he would not listen to anyone recounting how some public affair was being managed. Instead he took thought for how the soul might be perfected through virtue, and he bent his whole life to this with zeal, bidding farewell to the affairs of life. Here, quite simply, was another Moses in our own times, rivalling that man's wonders. Both went out of this turbulent and clamorous life, Moses and Gregory, each in his own time withdrawing to himself, until for both the gain of the pure life was made manifest through an appearance of God. But Moses had a wife who went along with him in his life of philosophy, whereas Gregory took virtue alone as his companion. Since, then, the aim was the same for both (for the goal of both in withdrawing from the crowd was to perceive the divine mysteries with the pure eye of the soul), anyone who knows how to look rightly at virtue may judge which of the two lived more free from passion: the one who stooped to the lawful and permitted share in pleasures, or the one who rose above even this and gave material attachment no way in against him. Now at that time Phaedimus

was leading the church of Amasea. He had from God, from the Holy Spirit, a certain power of foreknowledge, and he was making every effort to get the great Gregory into his hands and bring him to the government of a church, so that so great a good might not pass his life idle and unprofitable. But Gregory perceived the bishop's intention and contrived to stay hidden, moving from one wilderness to another. The great Phaedimus tried every attempt and used every device and stratagem, but he could not bring the man to the priesthood, for Gregory guarded with countless eyes against ever being caught by the bishop's hand. There was a zeal on both sides that matched the other: the one longed to catch him, the other to escape his pursuer. For the one knew that he would be bringing a holy offering to God, while the other feared that the care of the priesthood, laid on his life like a burden, might become a hindrance to philosophy. For this reason Phaedimus was lifted by a more divine impulse in the matter at hand. He paid no heed to the distance that separated him from Gregory (who was three days' journey away), but looked up to God and said that he and Gregory were alike seen by God at that hour. Then, in place of his hand, he laid his word upon Gregory. He consecrated to God one who was not bodily present, and assigned to him that city, which until those times had been so firmly held by the error of idols that, although the inhabitants of the city itself and of the surrounding country were countless, no more than seventeen were found who had received the word of faith. So Gregory took up the yoke under compulsion, and afterward all the customary rites were completed for him. He asked the one who had proclaimed him to the priesthood for a short time to come to an understanding of the precise truth of the mystery. He no longer thought, as the Apostle says, that he ought to confer with flesh and blood, but asked that the revelation of hidden things should come to him from God; and he did not venture on preaching the word until the truth had been revealed to him through some manifestation. For once, as he was pondering by night on the doctrine of faith and turning over all kinds of reasonings (for even then there were some who counterfeited the pious teaching and, through the plausibility of their arguments, often made the truth doubtful even to the wise), as he lay awake troubled over this, someone appeared to him, not in a dream but while he was awake, in human form: aged in appearance, priestly in the style of his garments, and displaying great virtue by the grace of his face

and the composure of his bearing. Gregory was struck with awe at the sight. He rose from his bed and asked to learn who he was and why he had come. The other calmed the turmoil of his mind with a gentle voice and said that he had appeared to him by divine command on account of the matters that were in dispute, so that the truth of the pious faith might be revealed. At these words Gregory took courage and looked at him with a kind of joy and amazement. Then the figure stretched out his hand straight in front of him, as though pointing with his outstretched fingers to something appearing to one side. Gregory followed the line of the hand with his own gaze, and opposite the one who had appeared he saw another vision, in the form of a woman, more than human. Struck with awe again, he bowed his face and was at a loss before the sight, unable to bear the apparition with his eyes. Indeed, the marvel of the vision lay chiefly in this: though it was deep night, a light shone out together with those who appeared to him, as if a bright lamp had been kindled. Since, then, he could not bear the apparition with his eyes, he heard a conversation between those who had appeared to him, as they discussed with each other the question he had been seeking to answer. Through this he was not only instructed in the true knowledge of the faith but also learned the names of those who had appeared, since each addressed the other by name. For he is said to have heard the one who appeared in the form of a woman urging John the Evangelist to reveal to the young man the mystery of godliness, and John replying that he was ready to grant this too to the mother of the Lord, since it was dear to her. Having then spoken the doctrine in well-proportioned and clearly defined form, he vanished again from sight. Gregory at once set down that divine initiation in writing. Afterward he preached the word in the church in accordance with it, and left that God-given teaching to those who came after him as a kind of inheritance. By it the people of that church are instructed to this day, and they have remained untouched by every heretical evil. The words of the initiation are these:

There is one God, Father of the living Word, of subsistent Wisdom and Power, and of the eternal Imprint; perfect Begetter of the perfect, Father of the only-begotten Son. There is one Lord, Only from Only, God from God, Imprint and Image of the Godhead, effective Word, Wisdom that embraces the structure of all things, and Power that makes the whole creation; true Son of the true Father, Invisible of Invisible, Incorruptible of Incorruptible, Immortal of Immortal, and Eternal of Eternal. And there is one Holy Spirit, who has his existence from God and has been manifested through the Son, that is, to humankind; perfect Image of the perfect Son, Life,

cause of the living, holy Fountain, Holiness, Giver of sanctification; in whom is manifested God the Father, who is over all and in all, and God the Son, who is through all. A perfect Trinity, neither divided nor estranged in glory, eternity and sovereignty. There is therefore nothing created or servile in the Trinity, nor anything brought in from outside, as though it did not exist before but came in later. So the Son was never lacking to the Father, nor the Spirit to the Son; but the same Trinity remains ever unchangeable and unalterable.

Whoever wishes to be convinced about this, let him listen to the church in which Gregory preached the word, among whose people the very letters written by that blessed hand are preserved even now. Does this not rival, in the magnificence of its grace, those tablets made by God? I mean those tablets on which the legislation of the divine will was engraved. For the Scripture says that Moses, having gone beyond what is visible and entered in his soul within the invisible sanctuary (this is what the darkness signifies), learned the divine mysteries and through himself led the whole people to the knowledge of God. The same dispensation can be seen in the case of this great man as well. His mountain was not something perceptible to the senses or an earthly hill, but the height of his desire for true doctrine; his darkness was the vision that others could not grasp; his tablet was his soul; and the letters on the tablets were the voice of the one who appeared to him. Through all these the revelation of the mysteries came both to him and to those he initiated. Through that vision, then, he was filled with boldness and courage. An athlete who has gained from his trainer enough experience and strength for the contests strips with confidence for the stadium and contends against his opponents. In the same way Gregory, having sufficiently anointed his soul both by his own study and by the alliance of the grace that had appeared to him, took up the contests. For his whole life in the priesthood should be called nothing other than contests and struggles, in which through faith he overcame all the power of the adversary.

As soon as he had roused himself from his remote retreat, he set out for the city where he was to establish the church for God. He learned that the whole region was held fast by the deceit of demons. No temple of the true God had been built anywhere, but the whole city and the surrounding country were full of altars, shrines and images. The whole nation was zealous that the precincts of the idols and their temples should be adorned, and that the madness for idols should remain among men, strengthened by processions and rites and the defilements upon the altars. So, like a brave soldier who engages the commander of the enemy line and through him puts to flight the troops under his command, this great man began his deeds of valour with the demons themselves. And how did this come about? As he was travelling the road from his retreat to the city, evening overtook him, and a rather violent rainstorm held him back,

[?] the smoke of sacrifices and the defilements, and to see again what he used to see before the demons were driven out of the temple. When these things had happened, the warden came to realize that Gregory had some divine power, by which he had shown himself stronger than the demons. He hurried after him again and overtook him before he reached the city, and asked to learn from him the mystery, and who that God was who held the nature of demons in subjection. When the great man had told him in a few words the mystery of godliness, the temple warden felt as anyone uninitiated in divine things might be expected to feel: he thought it beneath the idea of God to believe that the Divine had appeared to men in the flesh. Gregory replied that faith in this is not established by words but draws its credibility from the wonders that are done. The warden then asked to see yet another miracle from him, so that by what was done he might in this way be led to assent to the faith. Thereupon, it is said, that great man performed the great miracle that is the most incredible of all. The warden demanded that one of the huge stones visible before their eyes should be moved to another place without human hand, by the power of faith alone, at Gregory's command. And that great man, without the least delay, at once commanded the stone, as though it were alive, to move to the place the warden had pointed out. When this happened, the man immediately believed the word. He left everything—family, house, wife, children, friends, priesthood, hearth, possessions—and in place of all that he had, he chose to be with the great man and to share his labours and that divine philosophy and instruction.

Before this, let all the artful ingenuity of professional writers fall silent, which uses rhetoric to exaggerate wonders and exalt them into something greater. For the wonder in what has been told is not of a kind to become either less or greater than itself by the power of the speaker. What could anyone say beyond what has been said that would add to the wonder? And how could anyone lessen the hearers' astonishment at what took place? A stone draws away from stones those who were enslaved to stones; a stone becomes a herald of the divine faith and a guide to salvation for unbelievers. It proclaims the divine power not by any voice or word, but by what it did it shows the God whom Gregory preached, whom all creation obeys alike in subjection. Not only what is sentient, breathing and animate, but anything beyond these too receives the command of his servant as though it were not without sense. For what hearing does a stone have? What perception of the authority of the one commanding? What power of movement is in it? What structure of limbs and joints? Yet the power of the one commanding becomes all these things and more for the stone. Seeing this power, that temple warden at once recognized and abhorred the deceit the demons had worked on erring human nature, and went over to the true God, reckoning from what had been done by the servant

the inexpressible power of the Master. For if the servant's power is so great that he moves the immovable by a word, gives orders to things without sense, and issues commands to the lifeless, how great an abundance of power must one reasonably conceive in the Master of all, whose will became, as it were, the matter, the structure and the power of the world itself, of all that is in it, and of all that is beyond it!

From this point that great man began his feats of valour against the demons. Leading the temple warden about with him as a kind of trophy over the defeated, and having struck the nation with awe beforehand through the report of what had happened, he now rode into the city with confidence and boldness. He did not make a show of chariots and horses and mules and a crowd of attendants, but went escorted on every side by his virtues as by a bodyguard. The inhabitants of the town poured out en masse, as though to view some novel spectacle, all eager to see who this Gregory was: a man who held authority like a king over those they considered gods, who carried off and led the demons by his command wherever he wished, driving them out of whatever place he pleased and settling them wherever he saw fit, as though they were slaves; and who brought with him their very servant, as though he had enslaved him by some authority—a man who had scorned the honour he formerly held and exchanged all his possessions for life with Gregory. While they all awaited him before the town in this frame of mind, when he came up to them, with everyone gazing intently at him, he passed by the people as though they were lifeless matter. He turned to none of those he met and walked straight on to the city, and so he amazed them far more, appearing to the onlookers even greater than his reputation. That a man entering a great city for the first time, with no prior acquaintance there, should not be overawed by so vast a crowd gathered on his account, but should look only to himself and to the road, as though walking through a desert, turning to none of those assembled around him—this seemed to people greater than the miracle of the stone. For this reason, although, as was said earlier, only a very few had accepted the faith before he took charge, he entered hemmed in on every side by those escorting him, as if the whole city honoured his priesthood. Now, as soon as he had taken up philosophy, he had freed himself of everything at once, as of a burden. He had none of the necessities of life—no field, no place, no house—but he was everything to himself (or rather, virtue and faith were his homeland, his hearth and his wealth). So when he was within the city, there was

no house anywhere for him to rest in, neither the church's nor his own. Those around him were in a commotion, perplexed about where he should lodge and with whom he might find shelter. "Why is this?" the teacher said to them. "Why are you perplexed about where to rest your bodies, as though you were outside God's shelter? Does God seem a small house to you, if in him we live and move and have our being? Or are you cramped beneath the roof of heaven, and are you looking for some other lodging besides it? Let your one concern be each person's own house, the one built by virtues and raised up on high. Let this alone grieve us, that such a dwelling should not be left unprepared for us. For the enclosure of earthly walls brings no gain to those who live by virtue. It is rather those defiled with vice who might reasonably be anxious for walls, because a house often becomes a cover for hidden shameful deeds. But for those whose life is devoted to virtue, the walls have nothing to hide."

As he was saying these things to those gathered around him, one of the notable men came up, ranked among the first in family, wealth and influence of every other kind; the man's name was Musonius. When he saw many eager for the same thing, each wanting to receive the man into his own house, he forestalled the others and snatched the favour for himself. He begged the great man to be his guest and to honour his house with his entrance, so that he himself might become more venerable and renowned in the rest of his life, as time handed down the memory of such an honour to later generations. Many others also ran up and begged for the same thing, but Gregory judged it right to grant the favour to the one who had asked first. He dismissed the others with friendly words, honouring them in return, and lodged with the one who had come first.

If the account of him is a plain and unadorned narrative, our discourse having willingly left out the embellishments that ingenuity invents for such matters, this itself would be no small testimony to those who judge rightly that the wonders of the man we are remembering are in no way magnified by invention, but that the mere remembrance of his deeds suffices for the most complete praise—like the natural beauty of a face that needs no elaborate adornment from the cosmetic art. Those already instructed in the word were few in number, but before the day was out and the sun had set, so many were added on that occasion that the number of believers was enough to make up a congregation. At dawn the people were again at the doors: the men themselves, and women and children, the aged, and any who suffered some affliction of the body from demons or from some other injury. And he, in their midst, in a manner fitting the need of each of those assembled, with the

…sharing himself out by the power of the Spirit: preaching, inquiring with people, admonishing, teaching, healing. Above all he drew the multitudes to the preaching because what they saw matched what they heard, and through both the marks of divine power shone out in him. His words amazed their hearing, and the miracles he worked for the sick amazed their sight. The mourner was comforted; the young man was brought to self-control; the old man was cared for with fitting words. Slaves were taught to be well disposed toward their masters, and those in power to be kind to those under them. The poor man was taught that virtue is the one true wealth, and that anyone who chooses may acquire it. The man who prided himself on his riches was admonished as he deserved, and taught that he was the steward of his possessions, not their owner. He gave women what suited them, children what fitted their age, and fathers what was proper to them. Becoming all things to all, and with the Spirit working alongside him, he gathered so great a people to himself so quickly that he set about building a church, and everyone helped with the work, giving both money and labor. This is the church whose foundations he laid. One of his successors, a man worthy of him, adorned it further, and it is still shown today. As soon as the great man took office he set it in the most conspicuous part of the city as a kind of foundation and base for his own priesthood, and he completed the work by a certain divine power, as later times bear witness. For in our own day a very severe earthquake once struck the city, and nearly everything was utterly destroyed: all its buildings, public and private alike, were left in ruins and desolate. That church alone remained unbroken and unshaken, so that this too made plain with what power the great man handled the affairs of his time. But these things were shown by divine power many years later, as testimony to the great man's faith. At the time, everyone in the city and the surrounding country was astonished at his apostolic miracles and believed that everything he said and did was said and done by divine power. So even in the disputes of daily life they thought no other court had more authority over them. Every lawsuit and every hopelessly tangled affair was resolved by his counsel. As a result, through his grace there was good order and peace for the whole community and for each person in it, and good things greatly increased in private and in public, since no wickedness broke into their harmony with one another. It may not be out of place, perhaps, to recall one of his judgments, so that, as the proverb says, the whole fabric may become clear to us from its hem. For divine Scripture too, though Solomon judged many cases for his subjects,

was content to display the man's whole understanding through a single one. That was when he judged between the two mothers. The wrong could not be proved, since each of them equally refused the dead child and laid claim to the living one, so he resolved to track down the hidden truth by a stratagem. For since there was no witness to the wrong, and suspicion of lying and of telling the truth weighed equally on each, he called on nature itself to bear witness to the truth, hiding the purpose of his mind behind a cunning threat. He gave what seemed an order: the bodies of the living child and the dead one were to be cut equally in two with a sword, and each woman given half of each child. In this way he handed the judgment of the matter over to the nature of truth. One woman gladly accepted the order and urged on the executioner. The other, moved in her mother's heart, admitted defeat and begged that the child be spared, for she would be grateful if the infant were saved by any means at all. The king took this as his test of the truth and awarded the winning verdict to the woman who had willingly given way. He reasoned that the woman who was unmoved by the child's slaughter stood accused by nature itself, and that she was pressing for its death because she was not its mother. What judgment of the great Gregory, then, shall we relate? Two brothers, young in years, had just divided their father's inheritance between them and were quarrelling over a single lake. Each was determined to have the whole of it, and neither would let the other share the property. The teacher was made arbiter of the case. When he came to the place, he applied his own laws to the arbitration. He tried to lead them to reconciliation, urging the young men to come to terms as friends and to value the gain of peace above the gain from the lake's revenue. For peace endures forever, for the living and the dead alike, while revenue gives only passing enjoyment and brings eternal condemnation for injustice. He said whatever else a man like him would likely say to calm the unruliness of youth. But his appeal had no effect. Their youth was inflamed and blazed up into anger, swollen by a greater hope of gain. On each side an army was raised from their dependents, a crowd of hands thirsting for blood, led by anger and youth, and a time was set for the clash. The battle was to break out between the two sides on the following day. But the man of God stayed on the banks of the lake, kept vigil through the night, and performed over the water a wonder like those of Moses. He did not split the deep in two with the stroke of a rod. Instead, by prayer he turned the whole lake at once

into dry land. At dawn he showed the lake to be solid ground, dry and without moisture, so that not even in its hollows was any trace of water left in what had been a sea before he prayed. Having judged the case in this way by divine power, he went back to his own place. For the young men, the verdict delivered by the deed put an end to their rivalry. Since the thing over which they had been preparing war on each other no longer existed, peace took the place of anger, and nature made herself known again in the brothers. Even now one can see clear signs of that divine verdict. All around what was once the lake, certain traces of the water's flooding are preserved to this day. And everything that was then deep water and lake bottom has been turned into groves, houses, meadows and plowland. In this judgment, I think, not even the famous Solomon himself would claim the first prize. What great achievement is it to save a nursing babe between the breasts of two mothers, when its survival was assured in any case, whether it was nursed by the woman who bore it or by the other? Compare that with securing the safety of two young men! They had only just entered on the business of life and were in the prime of youth. At the very flower of their age, anger had driven them mad toward murdering each other. Soon they would have presented a bitter spectacle to the people of that time, their hands armed against each other, with the prospect that either both would be killed by one another or one of them would certainly incur the pollution of fratricide. I pass over those drawn up on each side in equal anger, for whom the only limit to their attack on each other was the death of their opponents. Gregory, then, by his prayer annulled the sentence of death already ratified against them by the evil one's generalship. He reconciled nature to itself again, and turned their eagerness for slaughter into the joys of peace. How much more justly should he be admired for his judgment than the one who detected the harlot's crime? As for the miracle on the water — how the navigable expanse was suddenly turned to dry land, how the lake became a plain and a hollow, and how what once served the place as a sea now yields a harvest of crops — I think it better to keep silent about it than to recount it in words that cannot rise worthily to the [?]

For what have we learned among the recorded miracles that could stand comparison with this? Joshua the son of Nun stopped the flow of the Jordan, but only while the ark was in the water. When the people had crossed and the ark had passed over, he gave the river back its usual course. In the Red Sea the bed of the deep was stripped bare of water, as the sea was driven aside by the wind. But the miracle lasted only as long as the army took to pass over dry ground along the

seabed. After that the surface of the waters became one again [?], and what had been divided for a short while flowed back together. Here, however, what was done once remained as it was done, so that the passage of time does not make the miracle doubtful, since what can be seen bears continual witness to it. Such, then, is what is told and shown about the lake. After this, another miracle of the same kind is pointed out and remembered as his. A river flows through their region whose very name shows how rough and wild its current is. Those who live near it call it the Lycus, the 'Wolf', because it does so much damage. It comes down in great volume even from its sources in Armenia, since that country feeds it abundantly from the mountains above. Everywhere it runs in a deep channel along the foot of the cliffs, and it becomes much rougher still with the winter torrents, taking into itself all the streams that flow down from the mountains. On the level ground it passes through, it is often hemmed in by the banks on either side. Then it overflows the bank at some point on one side and floods all the land above with its waters. So the people who lived there were continually exposed to dangers they did not expect, as the river often burst into the fields in the dead of night, or even by day. As a result, not only were plants, seed and livestock destroyed by the rushing water, but the danger reached the inhabitants themselves, who were wrecked without warning in their own houses by the flood. The miracles the great man had already worked had become known throughout the whole nation. So the people who lived by the river in that area rose up — men, women and children, the whole population — and came to the great man as suppliants, begging him to give them some release from their troubles that was beyond all hope. For they said that through him God could do everything that is impossible for human devices and thought. They themselves had left undone nothing that lay within human counsel and strength. With stones and embankments, and whatever else is usually devised against such evils, they had done everything, but they could not hold back the onrush of the disaster. To move him to pity more than anything else, they asked him to see the disaster with his own eyes and learn that they could not move their homes elsewhere, and that death was always before them whenever the water rushed in. So he came to the place, for no reluctance ever held back his eagerness to do good. He needed no carriage, no horses, nothing else to carry him. Leaning on a staff, he made the whole journey on foot, and as he went he discussed the higher hope with those who walked with him. He always spent his time on these things as his chief concern, and made everything else secondary to this more precious pursuit. His guides pointed out where the stream had been turned from its course, and the sight itself revealed the disaster: the rush of the waters had gouged the place into a deep ravine. Then he said this to those

who had gathered: 'Brothers, it is not for human beings to set boundaries to the movement of water. To shut the rush of the waters within bounds is the work of divine power alone. For this is what the Prophet says to God: "You set a boundary which it shall not pass." Only to Christ, the Master of creation, is the nature of the elements subject, and it stays forever in whatever places it is assigned. Since, then, it is God who lays down the bounds for the waters, he alone by his own power could fetter the disorder of this river too.' After he had spoken, it was as if he were inspired by a more divine thought. He prayed aloud that Christ would come as his ally in the task before him, and he drove the staff he carried in his hand into the ground where the bank had been broken. The earth there was soaked and spongy, and it easily gave way deep down, yielding both to the weight of the staff and to the hand that drove it in. Then he prayed to God that the staff would become a kind of bar and barrier against the disorder of the waters, and went back home. The outcome showed that everything he did was worked by divine power. For not long afterward the staff took root in the bank and became a tree. The tree stood fixed as a boundary for the stream, and to this day it is a sight and a story for the local people. Whenever the Lycus is swollen with rain and torrents, as it usually is, and comes rushing along, rough and roaring fearsomely, it reaches the foot of the tree with the edge of its waters. Then it swells up again in the middle and draws its stream back, and as if afraid to come near the tree, it passes the spot with a curving wave. Such was the power of the great Gregory, or rather of God who worked the miracles in him. For the nature of the elements was shown to be subject to him, as it were, changing at his commands as he saw fit. So a lake was turned into land that bears wheat, and people built homes in the water's ravines, since the staff had made them safe. To this day the tree is called 'the Staff', a memorial of Gregory's grace and power kept for the local people for all time. Which of the prophets' miracles would you have me set beside these for comparison? Shall I mention the parting of the Jordan, which Elijah made by striking it with his mantle before he was taken up, and which Elisha, heir of his mantle and his spirit, made after him? But in those cases the water divided only for the prophets, at the moment of need, and the Jordan became passable

in its current. It parted its stream only far enough to let the prophets walk through on its dry bed, and in the time that followed it was the same for the rest of mankind as it had been before. But the Lycus, once driven back from its disorderly course, makes Gregory's miracle permanent, for it remains for all time afterward just as the great man's faith made it at the moment of the wonder. The purpose of what was done was not to amaze onlookers but to save the people who lived by the river. The miracle itself is equal, for the nature of water gives way equally to the prophets and to the imitator of the prophets. Yet, if I may speak boldly, what Gregory did surpasses theirs in kindness. Through it the safety of the people who lived by the river was secured, since the water was fettered once for all at that point in its course and has stayed in place ever since. Such miracles were spreading through every part of the country, and people believed they were worked by the power of faith in Christ. So everyone longed to share in the faith that such miracles attested. The preaching advanced everywhere, the mystery was at work, and zeal for the good grew stronger, as clergy were established among all peoples so that the faith might abound and grow through them all. Then an embassy came to him from a neighboring city, asking him to come to them and establish their church by ordaining clergy. The city was called Comana, and its whole population begged the great man to stay with them, asking this as a favor. He came to them and spent some days among them, and by what he did and said he kindled their desire for the mystery still more. The time came for their embassy to reach its goal and for someone to be appointed bishop of their church. Then the minds of all the men in authority turned to those who seemed to excel in eloquence, birth and other distinctions. They thought that, since the great Gregory had these qualities, the man who received this grace should not lack them either. The votes were divided many ways, as each man preferred a different candidate, and the great man waited for some counsel from God in the matter. Samuel is recorded to have been unimpressed by bodily beauty and stature when he chose a king, and to have sought a kingly soul, even if it was found in a despised body. In the same way Gregory paid no attention to the efforts made on behalf of each candidate. He looked to one thing only: whether anyone, even before being proclaimed, already bore the priesthood in his character through a careful life and virtue. While the others were presenting their candidates with praise, each putting forward his own man, Gregory urged them to consider those of humbler outward life as well. For it was possible that even among such people someone could be found

who was richer in soul than those of more distinguished life. One of the men presiding over the vote thought this judgment of the great man an insult and a mockery. Since the others had been judged by eloquence, rank and the visible testimony of their lives, and none had been accepted for the priesthood, were some from among the manual laborers to be thought more worthy of such a grace? Mocking him, the man came up to him and said, 'If this is what you command — that these men, the chosen of the whole city, be passed over, and someone from the rabble be taken up to preside over the priesthood — then it is time for you to call Alexander the charcoal-burner to the priesthood. If you like, let us all go over to him and the whole city agree in our votes.' He said this to disparage Gregory's view, and to find fault with the strictness he had shown toward the candidates already put forward by casting this mocking vote. But these words made the great man think that it was not without God that Alexander had come to be mentioned during the voting and the discussion. 'And who is this Alexander you have mentioned?' he asked. Then, amid laughter, one of those present brought the man into the middle of the gathering. He was clothed in filthy rags that did not even cover his whole body. His appearance showed his trade, for his hands, his face and the rest of his body were grimed from his work with charcoal. To everyone else, Alexander standing there in their midst in such a state was something to laugh at. But to that discerning eye what was happening before him caused great amazement. Here was a man in extreme poverty and neglect of his body, who seemed focused on his own inner self and to rejoice, as it were, in this appearance, which uneducated eyes found laughable. And so it was. He had not come to such a life because poverty forced him to. The man was a philosopher, as his later life made known, and loftier than the rest, so that he even attained martyrdom, finishing his course through fire. He tried, or rather made it his practice, to remain hidden. He was above the good fortune that most people strive for and counted this life as nothing, since he longed for the higher and true life. To achieve his aim of virtue as fully as possible, he contrived to hide what he was, concealing himself under the most dishonorable of trades as under a hideous mask. Besides, he was in the full bloom of youth, and he thought it dangerous to his aim of chastity to let the beauty of his body be seen, as if he were parading the good fortune nature had given him. For he knew that such display becomes for many the occasion of grievous falls.

So that he might neither come to any harm he did not want, nor give other people's eyes an occasion for passion, he of his own accord put on charcoal-burning like an ugly mask. Through it his body was trained in virtue by hard labour, his beauty was hidden under the grime of the coals, and at the same time whatever his labours earned him was set aside for the service of the commandments. When Gregory had taken him aside from the assembly and learned everything about him in detail, he handed him over to his attendants and told them what to do. He himself went back to the assembly and taught those gathered there from the matter at hand, setting before them discourses on the priesthood and through them sketching the virtuous life. He went on with such discourses, keeping the assembly occupied, until the men who served him had done what they were told and appeared, bringing Alexander with them. He had washed off the unpleasant soot in a bath and was dressed in the great man's own clothes, for Gregory had ordered them to do this. Everyone turned towards Alexander and was amazed at the sight. "Nothing strange has happened to you," the teacher said to them. "Your eyes deceived you, because you left the judgement of beauty to the senses alone. Sense is an unreliable [?] judge of the truth of things, for by its very nature it shuts off the way into the depths of the mind. And at the same time this was exactly what the demon who is the enemy of piety wanted: that the chosen vessel should lie wholly idle, hidden under obscurity, and that a man who was to overthrow his dominion should never come forward." With these words he brought the man to God through the priesthood, consecrating him with grace in the customary way. Everyone fixed their eyes on the new priest, and when he was urged to address the church, Alexander showed at once, at the very start of his ministry, that the great Gregory had judged him truly. His speech was full of thought, though less adorned with the flowers of style. So one of the young men, an arrogant visitor from Attica who was staying among them, laughed at his plain diction, because it was not polished with Attic refinement. They say he was corrected by a vision from God: he saw a flock of doves shining with indescribable beauty, and heard someone say, "These are Alexander's doves, the ones you made a laughingstock." Which of these things should one admire more? That the man was not overawed by the vote of the dignitaries and not carried away by the testimony of the leading men? Or rather that he recognized the wealth hidden among the coals, to which God at once added his own testimony that the judgement was right, through the rhetorician's vision? To me each of them seems such in itself that they rival one another, and that both rank first among almost all the deeds remembered as marvels. For to stand against the pressure of the leading men [?]

was the clearest sign of a steadfast and lofty mind. In such a mind everything that appears in the world was regarded alike, whether it tended towards the greater and more conspicuous or towards the lowly and obscure. He gave preference to virtue alone, and judged only a life of vice to be worthless; everything else in life that is thought to deserve either eager pursuit or contempt he counted as nothing. And this is what he showed by what he did on that occasion. Seeking to find the one who was pleasing and worthy in God's sight, he did not think wealth, rank and worldly distinction trustworthy evidence, since the divine word counts none of these among the goods. So what deserves praise and wonder is not only that he would not give in to the eager wishes of the powerful, but also that by what he did next he surpassed even himself. Someone who merely rejects an unworthy candidate, but does not supply what the need requires, has prevented an evil but has not done any good. But he did not consent to the worse, and he also found the good; and so he completed the good in both ways, closing the way to evil and bringing the good into action. The great Gregory's benefaction to the city was therefore twofold: he corrected the error they had made through ignorance, and he brought to light the good that lay hidden among them. Since everything had gone as the great man intended, with the aid of the Holy Spirit, it would not be out of place to relate also an incident on the road, so that the grace that went with the man may be shown in every circumstance. It was plain to everyone that his chief concern was to direct everything towards the relief of those in need. So two Hebrews, whether looking for gain or plotting to bring some discredit on the man as easily taken in, lay in wait for his return. One of them pretended to be dead and lay stretched out on his back at the side of the highway. The other, as if wailing over the body, put on the cries of a mourner and called out to the great man as he passed, saying that this poor wretch had been suddenly carried off by death and lay there naked, with nothing ready for his burial. He begged the great man, holy soul that he was, not to pass him by, but to take pity on his poverty and give from what he had a last covering to be laid over the body. While the one was pleading with these and similar words, the other did not hesitate at all: he threw the double cloak he was wearing over the man lying there and went on his way. When he had gone past and the men who had played this trick on him were by themselves, the deceiver turned his pretended lament into laughter and told the man on the ground to get up, guffawing with delight at the gain their trick had brought them.

But the other lay in the same position, hearing nothing that was said. The man shouted louder and at the same time nudged him with his foot to rouse him, but the one lying there neither heard the voice nor felt the kick; he stayed stretched out just as before. For he had died the moment the cloak was thrown over him, and had truly met the death he had been faking to deceive the great man. So the man of God was not deceived after all: the cloak served those who received it for the very purpose for which he had given it. If such a deed seems grim for the faith and power of the great man, no one should be surprised, if he looks to the great Peter. For Peter too showed the power that was in him not only through his acts of kindness, as when he showed the people the man lame from birth running and leaping, or when he healed the illnesses of the sick with the shadow of his body, cast on them by the sun as it struck him from the side while the apostle passed by. He also condemned Ananias to death when he treated with contempt the power that dwelt in the apostle. He did this, I think, so that through fear of what happened to Ananias everyone among the people who was inclined to contempt might be brought to their senses by that fearful example, and be taught not to fall into the same sin. Fittingly, then, the imitator of Peter, who had shown the greatness of his power through many miracles of kindness, also made the man who tried to practise deceit against the Spirit tell the truth about himself. For it was right, I think, that the destroyer of falsehood should turn falsehood into truth even in the deceiver, so that it might be clear to everyone that whatever the great man said was true, and whatever he accepted as true was not false. So the Jews who, as they thought, had made a mockery of the great man's power in the way described became a lesson to others not to venture on deceit in matters where God himself becomes the accuser of what has been dared. After this, an assembly was once held in the open air at a place in the countryside. While everyone was listening to the teaching with wonder, a youth cried out to those standing round that it was not the teacher who was saying these things on his own: someone else was standing beside him and going through the words. After the assembly had broken up, the boy was brought to him, and the great man is said to have told those present that the youth was not free of a demon. At once he took the linen cloth from his shoulder, held it to the breath of his mouth, and then threw it over the young man. As soon as this was done, the youth began to be convulsed and to shout, to fall down and be thrown about, and to suffer everything that demons inflict. Then the saint laid his hand on him and calmed the convulsion. The demon flew out of him, and once he had returned to his right mind he no longer said that he saw the one speaking along with the saint.

This too is one of his great wonders: he performed his miracles of healing without any elaborate procedure. The breath of his mouth, brought to the sufferer through the linen cloth, was enough both to drive out demons and to heal the illnesses of the body. But to go through all his miracles one after another would take a long book, and a work beyond the leisure I have now. I will mention one or two more of the things told about him and end my account with these. By this time the divine preaching had spread everywhere, and everyone in the city and the surrounding country had turned to the pious faith of the true doctrine. Altars, temples and idols had been overthrown among them. Human life had already been cleansed of the pollutions of idolatry; the foul reek of sacrifices had been quenched, and the gore on the altars and the defilements of animal sacrifice had been washed away. Everywhere people were eagerly building houses of prayer in the name of Christ. Then rage and envy took hold of the man who ruled the Roman Empire at that time, because the ancestral objects of his deluded worship were being neglected, while the mystery of the Christians was growing, and the Church throughout the world was increasing in number and growing in size through those who were continually being added to the word. Thinking that he could set his own bitterness against the power of God, check the preaching of the mystery, break up the congregations of the churches, and turn back to the idols those who had come over to the word, he sent an order to the governors of the provinces. In it he set a fearful threat of punishment against them unless they maimed with every kind of torture those who worshipped the name of Christ, and brought them back, through fear and the compulsion of torture, to the ancestral worship of demons. This fearful and godless proclamation was announced to the governors, for the agents appointed by the tyrant's cruelty for this very purpose spread through the whole empire. Now the man who governed the province there was such that he needed no prompting from higher authority for this wicked undertaking, since he had by nature a cruelty and bitterness of his own, and a hostility towards those who believed in the word. He issued fearful public edicts that people must abjure the faith, or else be punished with every kind of penalty and death. At that time those in charge of public affairs did and pursued nothing else, publicly or privately, except to hunt down and punish those who held fast to the faith. The terror lay not only in the threats that were spoken; besides these, the elaborate apparatus of torture caused utter consternation and

struck fear into people before they had even felt it. Swords and fire, wild beasts and pits, instruments for wrenching the limbs, iron chairs set over fire, upright stakes on which the bodies of those who resisted were stretched and torn by the strokes of dreadful claws, and countless other devices invented for every kind of bodily torment were contrived by them. Those who held these offices had only one aim: that none of them should prove milder than another in the excess of his bitterness. Some informed, others pointed people out, others searched for those in hiding. Some attacked those who fled; others, with their eyes on the property of the faithful and hoping to get hold of their goods, harried those who held to the faith under the pretext of piety. There was utter confusion throughout the province and great helplessness, since everyone was suspicious of everyone else. Fathers could not count on their children's affection in those terrors, nor did nature guarantee children the loyalty of a father's care. Families were divided against one another, split by their religions. A son who followed the pagans betrayed his believing parents, and a father who remained in unbelief accused his believing son. A brother, for the same reason, made war on nature, thinking it a holy thing to have his own kin punished if he held fast to piety. So the deserts were full of the hunted, and the houses empty of those who lived in them. Many public buildings were given over to holding those who were locked up, for the prisons were not large enough to contain the multitude being punished for the faith. All the marketplaces and gatherings, public and private, instead of their usual cheerfulness took on calamities like these: some people being dragged off, others led away, and others either laughing or weeping at what was happening. The enemies felt no pity for infants, no reverence for grey hair, no respect for virtue; as in a captured city, every age was handed over to the enemies of the faith. Nor did the natural weakness of their sex allow women to remain free of these compulsions. There was a single law of cruelty for all, which subjected to the same measure of punishment anyone who had turned away from the idols, without regard to sex. Then the great man saw the weakness of human nature, and that the many would not be able to fight for piety to the point of death. So he advised the Church to give way a little before the fearful onslaught, thinking it better for them to save their souls by flight than to stand in the battle line of the contest and become deserters from the faith. And so that people might be fully persuaded that saving one's faith by flight brought no danger to the soul, he advised withdrawal by his own example, withdrawing himself before the others from the onrush of danger. At the same time, those in power were especially eager to capture him, as they would a general, in order to break up the whole battle line of the faith, and for this

reason the enemies were eager [?] to get him into their hands. He had taken refuge on a deserted ridge, with him the man who had at first been brought to the faith from serving as a temple warden, and who was by now serving in the grace of the diaconate. His pursuers followed on his track in great numbers, for someone had told them where he was hiding. Some of them surrounded the foot of the ridge and kept watch, so that he would have no way of escape anywhere if he tried to flee. Others climbed the mountain, searching every part of it, and were already in sight of the great man, running straight up towards him. He told his companion to stand firm before God with steady, unwavering confidence and to entrust his safety to him, stretching out his hands in prayer, and not to let fear drive out his faith even if the pursuers came close. He made himself an example of what he commanded for the deacon, gazing up to heaven with unmoving eyes, standing upright with his hands outstretched. So the two of them stood. The pursuers ran up to where they were and looked all round the place, searching with the greatest care every thicket, every jutting rock and every hollow of the ravines. Then they went back down to the foot of the hill, thinking that the men they were searching for had taken to flight in fear and had fallen into the hands of those posted round below. But he had not been found by those above, and he was not among those below. The informer, however, had observed the place where the great man was staying and marked it with signs; and at that spot the searchers insisted they had seen no one, only two trees standing a little apart. When the searchers had gone away, the informer stayed behind and found the great man and his companion at prayer. Recognizing the divine protection by which they had appeared to the pursuers as trees, he fell at his feet and believed the word; and the man who a little earlier had been a persecutor became one of the fugitives. They remained in the wilderness for a long time, since the war against the faith continued, with the governor raging fiercely against those who had joined the word of piety, and everyone had taken to flight. Since the persecutors had given up hope of the great man, convinced he would never fall into their hands, they turned their frenzied madness against the rest. Throughout the province they hunted down everyone alike, men, women and children, to whom the name of Christ was sacred. They dragged them to the city and filled the prisons, making their piety a charge against them in place of any other crime. So the courts at that time attended to no public business; the only thing the rulers cared about was to inflict every kind of torture and every sort of racking, by ever new [?] devices, on those who held fast to the faith.

It was here that it became even clearer to everyone that the great man did nothing without God's guidance. For by preserving himself for the people through his flight, he became a common ally to all who were contending for the faith. We hear of Moses that, standing far off from the battle against the Amalekites, he gave his own people strength against their enemies through prayer. In the same way Gregory, as though watching events with the eye of his soul, called down divine help on those who were struggling in the confession of the faith. Once, while he was praying to God with his companions as usual, he was suddenly filled with strain and agitation. It was plain to those present that he was as if astonished and in anguish at some spectacle, and he held his hearing intent, as though some sound were reaching him. A long interval passed, and all that time he remained unbending and motionless. Then, as though the spectacle before him had come to a good end, he returned to his normal state and praised God in a most radiant voice, uttering the hymn of victory and thanksgiving that we often hear David sing in the Psalms: "Blessed be God, who has not given us as prey to their teeth." Those around him were amazed and asked to learn what the sight before his eyes had been. He is said to have told them that at that hour he had seen a great fall: the devil had been thrown down by a young man in the contests for piety. When they still did not understand what he meant, he explained more plainly that at that hour a young man of noble birth, aided by a higher power, had fought the hard contest of faith after being brought before the governor by the executioners. He added the name too, calling him Troadius, and said that after many tortures, which he had nobly endured, he had won the crown of martyrdom. The deacon was astonished at what he heard. He did not dare to disbelieve anything that was said, yet he thought it beyond human nature that a man far from the city, to whom no one had reported anything, should tell his companions what had happened there as though he had been present at the events. So he begged his teacher to allow him to see with his own eyes and learn what had been done, and not to stop him from going to the very places where the wonder had taken place. Gregory said it was a fearful thing to go among the murderers, and that one could easily suffer some harm through the malice of the adversary. But the deacon said he took courage from the aid of his prayers, and spoke these words to him: "Commend me to God, and none of the enemies will easily lay hands on me." So Gregory sent God's help along with him through his prayer, like a travelling companion, and the deacon went on his way with confidence, paying no attention to anyone he met. He reached the city in the evening, and weary from the

[?]…of the journey, he thought it necessary to relieve his weariness with a bath. Now in that place a murderous demon held sway, haunting the bath. Its destructive power became active after dark against anyone who came near, and for this reason that bath could not be entered after sunset and stood unused. Standing before it, he asked the man in charge to open the door, to let him in, and not to begrudge him the refreshment of the bath. The attendant declared that none of those who dared the water at that hour had come back on their own feet: after evening the demon overpowered everyone, and many had already suffered irreparable harm through ignorance, and instead of the relief they had hoped for, laments and wailing had followed. Though he told him these and similar things, the stranger did not give up his desire at all, but pressed him in every way, insisting that he let him in. So the attendant, thinking it a gain not to share the danger brought on by the stranger's ignorance, left the key with him [?] and went off far from the bath. Once he was inside and had undressed, the demon contrived all sorts of means to frighten and terrify him. Apparitions of every kind appeared, showing a nature that was a mixture of fire and smoke. They rushed at his eyes in the shapes of men and beasts, rang in his ears, came close to his breath, and swirled in a circle around his body. But he held up the seal before himself, called on the name of Christ, and passed through the first room unharmed. When he went on into the inner room he met with still harsher sights, for the demon had changed into a more fearsome form. He thought the building was shaking as if in an earthquake, that the floor was splitting open to lay bare the fire below, and that fiery sparks were shooting up from the water. Again the same weapon, the seal and the name of Christ and the help of his teacher's prayers, scattered the terrors of what he saw and what was happening. When he had relaxed in the water and was hurrying to leave, he was hindered again, for the demon had laid hold of the door. But this obstacle too was removed of itself by the same power, as the door gave way before the seal. When everything had turned out as he wished, the demon is said to have cried out to him in a human voice not to count that power by which he had escaped destruction as his own, for it was the voice of the one who had commended him to the Guardian that had kept him from harm. Having been saved in this way, he astonished the keepers of the place, since none of those who had ever dared the water at that hour had been seen alive again.
