He told them what had happened to him, and learned that the heroic deeds of the martyrs in the city had come about in just the way the great man had described beforehand while living in the wilderness. Adding this to the accounts

and wonders concerning him (what he had seen, what he had heard, and what he had learned by his own experience about the power of the great man's faith, to which the demon had also borne witness), he hurried back to his teacher. To those of his own time and to later generations he left a common safeguard: that each person should commend himself to God through the priests. Even now this formula is used throughout the whole Church, and especially among those people, as a memorial of the help Gregory gave that man at the time. When that tyranny had been broken up with divine aid, and peace had returned to human life, so that zeal for the divine was free and open to all as they pleased, he went down to the city again. He travelled around the whole surrounding country and increased zeal for the divine among the peoples everywhere by establishing festivals in honor of those who had contended for the faith. The people divided the bodies of the martyrs among themselves, some in one place and some in another, and gathering each year as the annual cycle came round, they rejoiced and celebrated in honor of the martyrs. This too was a proof of his great wisdom. While reshaping his whole generation into a new life all at once, he stood over nature like a charioteer. He yoked them securely with the bridles of faith and the knowledge of God, and yet he allowed those under his rule to frisk a little under the yoke of faith for the sake of gladness. He saw that it was because of bodily pleasures that the childish and uneducated multitude clung to the error of idols. So, in order that the main thing might be achieved among them for the time being, namely that they should look to God instead of to vain objects of worship, he allowed them to make merry at the commemorations of the holy martyrs, to enjoy themselves and to rejoice. In time, he judged, their way of life would of its own accord change into something more dignified and more exact, with faith leading them toward it. And this has indeed already been achieved in most of them, since all their delight has passed from the pleasures of the body to the spiritual kind of gladness. This was how he conducted himself in the Church. He was eager, before his departure from this life, to see all the people converted from idols to the saving faith. So when he foresaw his own departure, he searched diligently through the whole surrounding region, wishing to learn whether any were still left outside the faith. He learned that those who still remained in the ancient error were no more than seventeen. Then, looking up to God, he said that this too was grievous, that anything should be lacking from the full number of the saved. Yet it was worthy of great thanksgiving that he was leaving to the one who would take over the Church after him as many idolaters as he himself had received Christians. Having prayed that those who already believed might grow toward perfection and that the unbelievers might be converted, he thus departed from human

life to God. He charged his close friends not to acquire a private [?] place for his burial. For if while living he had not accepted being called the owner of any place, but had spent his life as a sojourner on what belonged to others, he would certainly not be ashamed to be a sojourner after death. "Rather," he said, "let this be a story for later times: that Gregory was not named as owner of any place while he lived, and after death became a sojourner in the tombs of others." He had withdrawn himself from every possession on earth, so that he would not even accept burial in a place of his own, for he judged that the only precious possession was the one that bears no trace of greed. Let everyone who reads this account marvel at how the entire nation turned all at once from Greek vanity to the knowledge of the truth, and let no one disbelieve it, but look at the dispensation through which so great a change came about in those who passed from falsehood to truth. For I will now go back and relate what happened in the early days of his priesthood, which the narrative passed over in its haste to reach his other wonders. There was a public festival in the city, held according to an ancestral custom in honor of one of the local demons. Almost the whole nation flocked to it, and the entire countryside joined the city in the celebration. The theater was full of those who had streamed together, and the crowd of newcomers overflowed on every side above the seats. Since everyone was eager to look toward the orchestra for the spectacles and the performances, the stage was full of uproar and the performers' show came to nothing: the commotion of the crushed crowd not only cut short the enjoyment of the music but also gave the performers no chance to display their skills. Then a single cry burst from the whole populace, as they called on the demon whose festival they were holding and asked him to give them room. All were shouting together, the cry rose high, and the words seemed to come from the whole city as if from one mouth, offering this prayer to the demon. (The prayer, to give it in its very words, was: "Zeus, make room for us!") That great man heard the din of those calling on the demon by name and asking him to make room for the city. He sent one of those standing by to tell them that room would soon be given them, greater than they had prayed for. As soon as he had uttered this word, like a grim sentence, a plague overtook that public holy day. At once lament was mingled with the dances, so that their merriment was turned into mourning and calamity, and instead of pipes and clapping, dirge upon dirge took hold of the city. For once the disease had fallen on the people, it spread faster than anyone expected, feeding on the houses like fire, so that

the temples were filled with people wasting away from the disease who had fled there in hope of healing. Springs, fountains and wells were crowded with those burning with thirst in the helplessness of the illness. (For them the water could not quench the fever of the disease, since those once seized by it were the same after drinking as before.) Many made their own way to the tombs, and the survivors were no longer enough to bury the dead. Nor did the evil come upon people unexpectedly: an apparition would appear at the house that was about to be destroyed, and then destruction followed. So the cause of the disease became plain to all: the demon they had invoked was wickedly fulfilling the prayer of these fools, creating this evil "room" in the city through the disease. Then they became suppliants of the great man, begging him to halt the onrush of the evil through the God whom he knew and proclaimed, whom they now confessed to be the only true God, holding power over all. For since that apparition appeared before a house was to be destroyed, and at once brought despair of life, there was only one way of salvation for those in danger: for the great Gregory to come inside that house and drive out by prayer the disease that had fallen on it. Through those who first obtained such deliverance the report quickly spread to everyone. Then everything they had formerly pursued in their folly lay idle, oracles and purifications and their devotion to the idols, as all looked to the great priest and each one drew him to himself for the salvation of his whole household. His wage from those who were saved was the salvation of their souls. For once the priest's piety had been revealed by such proof, there was no more delay in assenting to the mystery among those who had been taught the power of faith through deeds. Thus for those people sickness proved stronger than health. As weak as their reasoning had been in health about accepting the mystery, so strong did they become in faith through bodily sickness. And so, once the error of idolatry had been exposed, all went over to the name of Christ. Some were led by the hand to the truth through the disease that had come upon them, while others held up faith in Christ as a protection against the plague. There are also other wonders of the great Gregory preserved in memory to this day, but we have not added them to what is written here, to spare incredulous ears, so that those who think the truth a lie because of the greatness of what is told may not be harmed. To Christ, who works such wonders through his servants, belong glory, honor and worship, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
